name: Cadotte’s aromatic polyamide composite reverse-osmosis membrane
description: John Cadotte made a reverse-osmosis membrane with a thin crosslinked aromatic polyamide separating layer formed on a porous support. Prototypes at the North Star Division of Midwest Research Institute and subsequent work at FilmTec led to the design described in US Patent 4,277,344.

date.label: November 1977
date.basis: The 1992 appellate opinion dates the experiments from evidence in the patent case.

events.statement: Cadotte tested aromatic polyamide composite prototypes at the North Star Division of Midwest Research Institute that removed salts from seawater.

evidence.supports: Finds that the November 1977 prototypes were tested and performed desalination.

date.label: 23 February 1978
date.basis: The appellate opinion specifies the day of the FilmTec experiments.

events.statement: At FilmTec, Cadotte tested related membranes with greater salt rejection than the November prototypes.

evidence.supports: Dates the follow-up test and describes the refinement of the same membrane design.

date.label: 7 July 1981
date.basis: Date of issuance on the US patent.

events.statement: US Patent 4,277,344 issued for Cadotte’s interfacially synthesized reverse-osmosis membrane.

evidence.supports: Documents the issue date and the aromatic polyamide composite structure.

earliest_record.rationale: The court record dates specific working prototypes for this aromatic polyamide design.

links.statement: The composite approach retained the thin selective layer and porous support of the Loeb–Sourirajan architecture, while letting developers form the two layers separately and choose their materials independently.

evidence.supports: The inventors introduce their composite development explicitly as an approach to improving the original Loeb–Sourirajan architecture.

evidence.locator: Background of the Invention, US 3,133,132 and US 4,277,344 discussion
evidence.supports: An independent membrane patent identifies the successive contributions and the separate input from interfacial polymerization.
Loeb distinguishes his integral asymmetric design from the composite approach developed by Francis, Cadotte and Riley.
The composite uses an aromatic polyamide separating layer formed on a porous support.
